title: 22. Interview: Cache Avalanche
summary: Interview Q&A for Cache Avalanche — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Cache Avalanche interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is cache avalanche, and how is it different from cache stampede and cache penetration?
**Answer:** Cache avalanche is when **many cache entries expire simultaneously** (or an entire cache crashes), causing a large burst of misses that overwhelms the database. Cache stampede (Topic 12) is when **one hot key** expires and many concurrent requests for *that key* hit the database — the difference is the number of keys involved: stampede = 1 key, avalanche = many keys. Cache penetration (Topic 13) is when requests for **non-existent keys** bypass the cache — the cache never had the value and never will, so the misses are perpetual (no repopulation helps). The triggers differ: avalanche is triggered by synchronized TTLs or cache crashes; stampede is triggered by a single hot key's TTL; penetration is triggered by absent keys (often malicious). The mitigations differ accordingly: avalanche needs TTL jitter (to spread expirations), never-expire policies (to remove expirations), RDBMS-backed hot-replica caches (to survive cache crashes), and circuit breakers (to contain the cascade); stampede needs singleflight, SWR, or XFetch; penetration needs null caching, Bloom filters, and rate limiting. The monitoring signatures also differ: avalanche shows a sudden hit-rate drop across many keys; stampede shows a sudden hit-rate drop for one key; penetration shows a sustained high miss rate with no recovery.
**Visual:**
```
Stampede:    1 hot key expires -> N concurrent requests -> N DB queries on 1 key
Avalanche:   N keys expire at once -> N misses -> N DB queries on N keys (DB overload)
Penetration: K (absent) -> cache miss -> DB NULL -> (cache nothing) -> repeats forever
```

### Q2. Why does TTL jitter prevent cache avalanche, and what is the right jitter range?
**Answer:** TTL jitter prevents avalanche by **spreading synchronized expirations** across a time window. Without jitter, if 100,000 keys are written at T=0 with TTL=3600s, they all expire at T=3600 — a synchronized peak. With jitter, each key gets `TTL = base_ttl + random(0, jitter_range)`, so expirations are spread across `[T=3600, T=3600+jitter_range]`. If jitter_range=600s (10% of base), the 100,000 expirations are spread over 10 minutes, producing a steady ~170 expirations/sec that the database easily absorbs. The right jitter range is a meaningful fraction of the TTL — typically 5–20%. Too small (1%): the peak is still sharp enough to cause a smaller avalanche. Too large (50%): the cache's effective TTL becomes too unpredictable, and some keys expire much earlier than expected (potentially causing stampede-like behavior on those keys). The 10% rule of thumb is a good default: `TTL = base * 1.10 + rand(0, base * 0.10)`. Jitter is universal (works with any cache, no coordination needed) and zero-cost (no extra latency, no extra memory), making it the first line of defense. The limitation: jitter only helps with synchronized TTLs — it does nothing for cache crashes (where the entire cache is lost at once). Real-world: Cloudflare adds 10% jitter to all CDN TTLs; Netflix's EVCache injects jitter into every write.
**Visual:**
```
No jitter (TTL=3600):
  T=0       write 100k keys (all TTL=3600)
  T=3600    100k keys expire simultaneously -> DB burst 100k QPS -> avalanche

With 10% jitter (TTL=3600+rand(0,360)):
  T=0       write 100k keys (TTL varies 3600..3960)
  T=3600    first key expires
  T=3600..3960  remaining 99,999 keys expire, spread over 6 min
            -> steady ~280 exp/sec -> DB load ~280 QPS (safe)

With 50% jitter (too much):
  T=0       write 100k keys (TTL varies 3600..5400)
  T=3600    first key expires (but user expected it to last 5400s)
            -> effective TTL unpredictable, some keys expire too early
```

### Q3. What is the "never expire" pattern, and what are its trade-offs?
**Answer:** The "never expire" pattern writes cache entries with **no TTL** (or a very long TTL as a safety net, e.g., 7 days), and uses a **background refresh job** to keep them up-to-date. Keys never actually expire (the refresh job re-fetches them from the database before they would), so there are no synchronized expirations and no avalanche. The trade-offs: (1) **Stale data** — the cache serves the value from the last refresh, which may be seconds or minutes stale. For read-heavy workloads where slight staleness is acceptable (product catalog, recommendation metadata, user display names), this is fine; for write-sensitive workloads (inventory counts, balances), it's not. (2) **Refresh-job complexity** — the job must know which keys to refresh (via `OBJECT FREQ` in Redis, access logs, or a manifest), handle failures gracefully (skip a key on error, retry later), and rate-limit refreshes (e.g., 1000/sec) to avoid overwhelming the database with refresh queries. (3) **Memory pressure** — without TTLs, keys are never evicted by expiration, only by LRU; the cache may grow larger than with TTLs, requiring more careful capacity planning. (4) **Operational overhead** — the refresh job is a new service to deploy, monitor, and debug. The pattern works best for **hot keys with stable values** (the top 1% of keys that account for 80% of traffic). Cold keys should still use TTLs (with jitter) so they expire naturally and free memory. Real-world: Facebook's TAO cache uses never-expire for graph edges; many CDNs use origin-pull-on-stale (a variant).
**Visual:**
```
Never-expire pattern:
  T=0      SET K = V (no TTL) -> stays forever
  T=60     refresh job: GET K from DB -> SET K = V' (no TTL)
  T=120    refresh job: GET K from DB -> SET K = V''
  ...      (K never expires, always serves latest refresh value)

  No synchronized expiration -> no avalanche
  Trade-off: K may be up to (refresh interval) stale (e.g., 60s)
  Memory: K stays in cache until LRU evicts it (not TTL)
```

### Q4. How does a circuit breaker limit the blast radius of a cache avalanche?
**Answer:** A circuit breaker monitors the database's health (query latency, error rate, connection pool saturation) and **opens** when the database starts to degrade — stopping all queries to the database for a cooldown period and returning a fallback response (stale cached value, default value, or 503 with Retry-After). This gives the database time to recover (the load drops to zero while the circuit is open), preventing the cascade from spiraling into a full outage. After the cooldown (e.g., 30s), the breaker **half-opens** — it allows a single probe query through; if it succeeds, the breaker **closes** and traffic resumes; if it fails, the breaker reopens for another cooldown. The circuit breaker does not *prevent* the avalanche (it does nothing about synchronized TTLs), but it *limits the blast radius* — instead of a 30-minute outage, you get a 30-second degraded window. The trade-off: the fallback response must be acceptable. Serving stale data is usually fine (users prefer a slightly stale page to a 500 error); serving a 503 is acceptable if the client retries gracefully (with exponential backoff). The breaker must also be tuned: too sensitive (opens on every transient spike) and you degrade service unnecessarily; too insensitive (opens only on total DB failure) and you don't catch the avalanche early enough. Real-world: Netflix's Hystrix (now Resilience4j) pioneered this pattern; Envoy and Istio provide circuit breakers at the service-mesh layer.
**Visual:**
```
Circuit breaker states:

  CLOSED (normal) -> queries flow to DB
    |
    | DB p99 > 1s for 5s (degradation detected)
    v
  OPEN (tripped) -> queries blocked, return fallback
    |
    | after 30s cooldown
    v
  HALF-OPEN -> 1 probe query allowed
    |
    |-- success -> CLOSED (traffic resumes)
    |-- failure -> OPEN (another 30s cooldown)
```

### Q5. How would you design a cache cluster to survive a complete cache crash (all nodes lost)?
**Answer:** A complete cache crash (e.g., the entire Redis cluster dies) is the worst-case avalanche: every key is lost at once, so 100% of traffic misses. The defenses, in order of priority: (1) **Multi-AZ replication** — run the cache in at least 3 availability zones with synchronous replication, so a single-AZ failure doesn't lose data. Redis Cluster and Memcached (with client-side consistent hashing) support this. (2) **Hot-replica fallback cache** — maintain a secondary cache (smaller, e.g., the top 1% of hot keys) in a separate cluster or in-process (Caffeine). If the primary cache misses, fall back to the secondary; if both miss, hit the database. The secondary absorbs the bulk of miss traffic because hot keys account for 80%+ of requests. (3) **Circuit breaker on the database** — if the database starts to degrade from the miss surge, the breaker opens and serves stale/503 responses, preventing a cascade. (4) **Pre-warming** — after the cache crashes, a background job pre-warms the hot keys from the database (rate-limited) before traffic returns to normal. (5) **Client-side retries with exponential backoff** — clients should retry on 503 with jittered backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, max 30s) to avoid thundering-herd retries when the cache recovers. (6) **Graceful degradation** — the application should have fallback paths for non-critical data (e.g., serve a default product image if the personalized one is unavailable). The combination turns a 30-minute outage into a 30-second degraded window. Real-world: Netflix's EVCache runs multi-region with cross-region replication; Amazon's DynamoDB caches use multi-AZ with hot-replica fallback.
**Visual:**
```
Cache crash defense (layered):

  Client request
   |
   v
  [Primary cache cluster, 3 AZs, sync replication]
   |-- miss (cluster crashed)
   v
  [Secondary hot-replica cache, top 1% of keys]
   |-- miss (not in top 1%)
   v
  [Database with circuit breaker]
   |-- CB open -> return stale / 503 (degraded but alive)
   |-- CB closed -> query DB, return value
   v
  [Pre-warming job] rebuilds primary cache in background
```

### Q6. What is a cold-start avalanche, and how do you prevent it after a deploy?
**Answer:** A cold-start avalanche occurs when the cache is empty after a deploy, restart, or flush — every key misses simultaneously, so the database sees 100% of traffic instead of the steady-state 1% miss rate. The trigger is different from a TTL-synchronized avalanche (no expiration event), but the effect is the same: the database is overwhelmed. The prevention is **pre-warming**: a background job identifies the hot keys (via access logs, `OBJECT FREQ` in Redis, or a manifest of known-hot keys), fetches them from the database in batches (rate-limited to e.g., 1000/sec to avoid overwhelming the DB during pre-warming), and writes them to the cache **before** cutting traffic over to the new deployment. The implementation: (1) Deploy the new code version but don't route traffic to it yet (blue-green deploy or canary). (2) Run the pre-warming job on the new deployment's cache. (3) Once the cache is warm (top 1,000 or 10,000 keys populated), gradually shift traffic to the new deployment (canary: 1%, 10%, 50%, 100% over 10 minutes). (4) Monitor the cache hit rate during the shift; if it drops below 90%, pause the shift and let the cache catch up. The trade-off: pre-warming adds 30–60s to the deploy pipeline (the pre-warm duration), but it eliminates the cold-start avalanche entirely. Real-world: Netflix's EVCache pre-warms after every deploy; most CDN deployments pre-warm the edge POPs for popular content; Stripe's idempotency cache pre-warms on failover.
**Visual:**
```
Cold-start avalanche (no pre-warming):
  T=0    Deploy v2 -> cache empty -> route 100% traffic to v2
  T=0    100% miss -> 100k QPS on DB -> DB crashes -> 30min outage

With pre-warming:
  T=0    Deploy v2 (no traffic yet)
  T=0    Pre-warm job: fetch top 10k hot keys from DB, rate-limited 1k/sec
  T=10s  Cache warm (10k hot keys populated) -> route 1% traffic to v2
  T=11s  Hit rate 99% -> route 10% -> hit rate 99% -> route 50% -> 100%
  T=60s  Fully shifted, no avalanche, no outage
```

### Q7. How do you monitor for cache avalanche, and what are the early warning signs?
**Answer:** The monitoring for cache avalanche focuses on three signals: **cache hit rate**, **database QPS**, and **database latency**. The signature of an avalanche is a sudden drop in cache hit rate (from 99% to <50%) accompanied by a spike in database QPS and database latency. The early warning signs, in order of severity: (1) **Hit rate drop**: a sustained drop below 95% (or 5 percentage points below the baseline) for more than 1 minute suggests expirations are outpacing repopulation. (2) **Database QPS spike**: a 2x or more spike in database QPS over 30 seconds suggests the cache is missing more than usual. (3) **Database latency spike**: p99 latency exceeding 1s (or 5x the baseline) suggests the database is saturating — this is the avalanche-in-progress signal, and the circuit breaker should trip. (4) **Connection pool saturation**: if the database's connection pool is at 90%+ utilization, the next miss surge will exhaust it. (5) **Cache memory pressure**: if the cache's eviction rate spikes, keys are being evicted before their TTLs (LRU pressure), which causes premature misses. The alerts should be: hit rate < 90% (warning), hit rate < 70% (critical), database p99 > 1s (critical), circuit breaker open (critical). The dashboard should show hit rate, database QPS, database latency, cache memory usage, and eviction rate on the same time axis, so the correlation is visible. Real-world: Netflix's EVCache dashboard shows all five metrics; Datadog and Prometheus have pre-built Redis dashboards with these signals.
**Visual:**
```
Avalanche monitoring dashboard (time series):

  Hit rate     |  DB QPS     |  DB p99    |  CB state
  ------------ | ----------- | ---------- | ---------
  99% (normal) | 100 (norm)  | 5ms (norm) | CLOSED
  99%          | 100         | 5ms        | CLOSED
  85% (drop!)  | 500 (spike) | 50ms       | CLOSED  <-- early warning
  60% (crit!)  | 2000        | 800ms      | CLOSED  <-- avalanche starting
  30% (crit!)  | 5000        | 5000ms     | OPEN    <-- CB trips, contain
  90%          | 200         | 50ms       | HALF    <-- recovering
  99%          | 100         | 5ms        | CLOSED  <-- recovered
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your team deploys a new version of the service every Tuesday at 2am. After every deploy, the database CPU spikes to 100% for 5 minutes. What's happening and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** This is a textbook **cold-start avalanche** — the deploy flushes the cache (either explicitly via a `FLUSHDB` or implicitly because the new code uses different cache keys), so the first wave of traffic after the deploy sees 100% misses and hits the database. The 5-minute spike is the time it takes for the cache to repopulate from the steady-state traffic (the hot keys get cached as requests come in, but during the warm-up the database absorbs everything). The fix is **pre-warming**: after the deploy but before routing traffic, run a background job that fetches the hot keys (top 1,000 or 10,000 by access frequency) from the database and writes them to the cache, rate-limited to e.g., 1000/sec to avoid overwhelming the database during pre-warming. Once the cache is warm (10-30 seconds), gradually shift traffic to the new deployment (canary: 1%, 10%, 50%, 100% over 5 minutes) and monitor the hit rate; pause the shift if the hit rate drops below 90%. The pre-warming job can use access logs from the previous deployment to identify the hot keys, or `OBJECT FREQ` in Redis (with LFU eviction). The trade-off: pre-warming adds 30-60s to the deploy pipeline, but eliminates the 5-minute database spike. Real-world: Netflix's EVCache pre-warms after every deploy; Amazon's deploy pipelines include a cache-warm step.
**Visual:**
```
Before (no pre-warming):
  T=0    Deploy v2 -> FLUSHDB -> route 100% traffic -> 100% miss -> DB 100% CPU
  T=5min Cache warm (from traffic) -> DB CPU returns to normal

After (with pre-warming):
  T=0     Deploy v2 (no traffic)
  T=0     Pre-warm: fetch top 10k hot keys, rate-limited 1k/sec
  T=10s   Cache warm -> route 1% traffic -> hit rate 99% -> route 10% -> 50% -> 100%
  T=5min  Fully shifted, DB CPU stays at 5% throughout
```

### Q2. Your product catalog cache uses TTL=3600s. Every hour on the hour, the database CPU spikes from 10% to 90% for about 30 seconds. Diagnose and fix.
**Answer:** The hourly spike aligned with the TTL is a textbook **TTL-synchronized avalanche** — the cache is being bulk-refreshed (probably by a cron job that runs at the top of each hour to update the catalog), and all the keys are written with the same TTL=3600s, so they all expire at the next top-of-the-hour. The 30-second spike is the window during which the expired keys are being repopulated, and during that window the database absorbs the miss traffic. The fix is **TTL jitter**: change the TTL from `3600` to `3600 + random(0, 600)` (10% jitter). This spreads the expirations across a 10-minute window (from T=3600 to T=4200), so the database sees a steady ~170 misses/sec instead of a synchronized burst. The jitter should be applied at write time: when the cron job writes a key to the cache, it should set `TTL = 3600 + random.randint(0, 600)`. The trade-off: some keys will expire up to 10 minutes later than they would have without jitter, meaning slightly staler data for those keys; for a product catalog (which changes infrequently), this is acceptable. If staleness is a concern, use a shorter jitter range (5%) or pair jitter with the never-expire pattern (refresh keys in the background before they expire). The fix is a one-line code change and eliminates the spike immediately. Real-world: Cloudflare adds 10% jitter to all CDN TTLs specifically to prevent this pattern.
**Visual:**
```
Before (TTL=3600, no jitter):
  T=0:00    Cron refreshes 10k catalog keys, all TTL=3600
  T=1:00    All 10k keys expire simultaneously -> 10k DB queries in 30s -> CPU 90%
  T=1:00:30 Cache repopulated -> CPU returns to 10%
  T=2:00    Repeat

After (TTL=3600+rand(0,600)):
  T=0:00    Cron refreshes 10k keys, TTL varies 3600..4200
  T=1:00    First key expires -> 1 DB query
  T=1:00..1:10 Remaining 9999 keys expire, spread over 10 min
            -> steady ~17 misses/sec -> CPU stays at 12% (barely noticeable)
```

### Q3. A marketing campaign is launching at 9am. You expect a 10x traffic surge. How do you prevent a cache avalanche?
**Answer:** The campaign launch is a known event, so you have time to prepare. The risk is twofold: (1) **Cold-start avalanche** if the cache is empty at 9am (the first surge of traffic sees 100% misses); (2) **Synchronized TTL avalanche** if the campaign-specific keys (e.g., the campaign landing page, promotional products) are all written at 9am with the same TTL. The defenses: (1) **Pre-warm the cache before 9am** — identify the campaign-specific hot keys (the landing page, the featured products, the recommendation lists) and fetch them from the database at 8:55am, writing them to the cache with jittered TTLs. This ensures the cache is warm when the surge hits at 9am. (2) **Use TTL jitter on all campaign keys** — `TTL = 3600 + rand(0, 600)` so their expirations are spread, preventing a synchronized avalanche at 10am. (3) **Scale the cache cluster vertically** before the launch — add more memory and shards to handle the increased working set (the campaign may bring new hot keys that weren't in the cache before). (4) **Scale the database read replicas** — add 2-3 extra read replicas to absorb the increased miss traffic during the launch window. (5) **Enable the circuit breaker** on the database with a conservative threshold (e.g., trip if p99 > 500ms) so a cascade is contained. (6) **Monitor closely during the launch** — have an engineer on-call with a dashboard showing hit rate, DB QPS, DB latency, and CB state; be ready to throttle traffic (rate-limit at the edge) if the system degrades. (7) **Have a rollback plan** — if the campaign causes an outage, disable the campaign landing page and revert to the static fallback. Real-world: Amazon Prime Day and Black Friday campaigns use this exact playbook.
**Visual:**
```
T=8:55  Pre-warm cache: fetch 50 campaign hot keys, TTL=3600+rand(0,600)
T=8:55  Scale cache cluster: +2 shards (more memory for campaign keys)
T=8:55  Scale DB read replicas: +3 replicas (absorb miss traffic)
T=8:55  Enable circuit breaker: trip if DB p99 > 500ms
T=9:00  Campaign launches -> 10x traffic surge
T=9:00  Hit rate 99% (cache warm) -> DB load stays at 2x (not 10x)
T=9:00  Engineer monitors dashboard, ready to throttle if needed
T=10:00 TTLs start expiring (jittered) -> steady ~5 misses/sec -> no avalanche
```

### Q4. Your Redis cluster crashed and was restarted. Now the database is at 100% CPU. What do you do?
**Answer:** This is a **cache-crash avalanche** — the Redis restart lost all keys (if persistence wasn't enabled or the restart was fast enough that AOF didn't replay), so 100% of traffic misses and hits the database. The immediate actions, in order: (1) **Trip the circuit breaker manually** (or confirm it auto-tripped) to stop the database from receiving more queries — return 503 with Retry-After to clients, or serve stale fallbacks if available. This stops the cascade and lets the database recover. (2) **Check if Redis had persistence enabled** — if AOF or RDB was on, Redis may be replaying the persistence file and will repopulate the cache in a few minutes; in that case, just wait and gradually restore traffic. (3) **If persistence was off or the file is corrupted**, run the pre-warming job: fetch the top 1,000-10,000 hot keys from the database (rate-limited to 1000/sec) and write them to Redis. This rebuilds the hot-key cache in 10-30 seconds. (4) **Gradually restore traffic** — once the cache has the hot keys, shift traffic back in stages (10%, 50%, 100%) and monitor the hit rate; pause if it drops below 90%. (5) **Investigate the crash** — check Redis logs (OOM, fork failure, network partition), and address the root cause (add memory, enable persistence, add replicas for HA). (6) **Post-mortem**: enable Redis Cluster with multi-AZ replication and AOF persistence so the next crash doesn't lose data; add a hot-replica fallback cache (Caffeine in-process) for the top 1% of keys; ensure the circuit breaker is configured to auto-trip on DB degradation. Real-world: Netflix's EVCache runs multi-region with cross-region replication; if one region's cache crashes, the other region serves the hot keys.
**Visual:**
```
T=0     Redis crashes -> all keys lost -> 100% miss -> DB 100% CPU
T=0:01  Circuit breaker auto-trips -> DB load drops to 0 -> DB recovers
T=0:01  Check Redis persistence: AOF disabled, no recovery possible
T=0:01  Run pre-warm job: fetch top 5k hot keys from DB, rate-limited 1k/sec
T=0:06  Redis warm (5k hot keys) -> 80% of traffic hits cache
T=0:06  Restore traffic: 10% -> hit rate 95% -> 50% -> 99% -> 100%
T=0:10  Fully restored, DB CPU at 10%
T=0:30  Post-mortem: enable AOF, add replicas, add hot-replica fallback
```

### Q5. Your service uses a never-expire cache for hot keys, but the database is still overloaded. Investigations show the refresh job is querying the database too aggressively. What do you do?
**Answer:** The never-expire pattern shifts the load from "miss-driven queries" to "refresh-driven queries" — instead of the database serving misses on demand, it serves the refresh job's periodic queries. If the refresh job runs too frequently or refreshes too many keys, it can overload the database just as much as the avalanche it was meant to prevent. The fixes: (1) **Rate-limit the refresh job** — cap the refresh rate at e.g., 1000 queries/sec, so even if there are 100,000 keys to refresh, the job takes 100 seconds (not 1 second of 100k QPS). (2) **Refresh based on access frequency** — use Redis's `OBJECT FREQ` (with LFU eviction) to identify the truly hot keys, and refresh only those (e.g., the top 1,000 keys), not all 100,000. Cold keys don't need refreshing because they're rarely read. (3) **Increase the refresh interval** — if the refresh job runs every 60s, change it to every 300s; the cache will be up to 5 minutes stale, but the database load drops 5x. For most hot-key workloads (product catalog, user display names), 5-minute staleness is acceptable. (4) **Batch the refresh queries** — instead of one query per key, use a `WHERE id IN (...)` query to fetch 100 keys in one round-trip, reducing the query count by 100x. (5) **Offload the refresh to a read replica** — point the refresh job at a read replica instead of the primary database, so the refresh load doesn't compete with user traffic. (6) **Monitor the refresh job's database load** — track the queries/sec the job generates, and alert if it exceeds the budget (e.g., 10% of the database's capacity). The lesson: the never-expire pattern is not free — it shifts load from misses to refreshes, and the refresh job must be tuned to stay within the database's capacity.
**Visual:**
```
Before (refresh job too aggressive):
  Refresh job runs every 60s, refreshes all 100k keys
  -> 100k queries / 60s = 1666 QPS sustained on DB
  -> DB CPU 80% from refresh job alone -> overloaded

After (tuned refresh job):
  Refresh job runs every 300s, refreshes only top 1k hot keys (by OBJECT FREQ)
  -> 1000 queries / 300s = 3.3 QPS sustained on DB
  -> DB CPU 1% from refresh job -> safe
  -> Trade-off: cold keys may be stale (but they're rarely read, so OK)
```

### Q6. You're using Redis Cluster with 3 shards. One shard crashes, and the database load spikes. Why, and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** Redis Cluster shards (or any sharded cache) partition the keyspace — each shard owns a subset of keys (e.g., shard 1 owns keys hash-slot 0-5460, shard 2 owns 5461-10922, shard 3 owns 10923-16383). When one shard crashes, all keys in its hash slots are lost — but the cluster doesn't fail over to the database; it either redirects requests to a replica (if configured) or returns errors for the affected hash slots. The database load spike happens because: (1) If the application doesn't handle the shard failure gracefully, it may treat the errors as cache misses and fall through to the database for every request to the affected hash slots — turning 1/3 of traffic into database queries. (2) If a replica is promoted (failover), there's a brief window (10-30s) where the affected hash slots are unavailable, and during that window the application may fall through to the database. The fixes: (1) **Configure Redis Cluster with replicas** — each shard should have at least one replica, so if the primary crashes, the replica is promoted automatically (typically in 10-30s). This is the standard HA setup. (2) **Use multi-AZ deployment** — spread the shards and replicas across availability zones, so an AZ failure doesn't take down a whole shard (primary and replica). (3) **Handle cache errors correctly** — the application should distinguish between "cache miss" (key not present, fall through to DB) and "cache error" (shard unavailable, return fallback or 503, do NOT fall through to DB). Falling through to DB on cache errors causes the avalanche. (4) **Add a circuit breaker** — if the database load spikes (from the failover window or from incorrect error handling), the breaker trips and protects the database. (5) **Monitor shard health** — alert if any shard's primary is down or if a failover is in progress. Real-world: AWS ElastiCache and Redis Enterprise provide managed Redis Cluster with automatic failover.
**Visual:**
```
Redis Cluster (3 shards, each with 1 replica, multi-AZ):

  Shard 1 (slots 0-5460)      Shard 2 (slots 5461-10922)  Shard 3 (slots 10923-16383)
  [Primary] [Replica]         [Primary] [Replica]         [Primary] [Replica]
     AZ-A      AZ-B              AZ-B      AZ-C              AZ-C      AZ-A

  Shard 1 primary crashes (AZ-A failure):
  -> Replica in AZ-B promoted (10-30s failover)
  -> During failover: requests to slots 0-5460 should return 503 (NOT fall to DB)
  -> After failover: replica serves normally, no DB impact

  Without replica:
  -> Shard 1 down -> slots 0-5460 unavailable -> if app falls through to DB,
     1/3 of traffic hits DB -> DB load spike (avalanche on 1/3 of keyspace)
```

### Q7. Your team enabled TTL jitter, but you still see periodic avalanches. Investigations show they align with a daily batch job that rewrites the entire cache. What's wrong and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** The TTL jitter is correctly spreading the expirations *within each batch*, but the batch job rewrites the entire cache daily — meaning all keys are written at the same time (the batch run time) with jittered TTLs. The jitter spreads expirations across the jitter window (e.g., 10 minutes), but the *next* batch run rewrites all keys again, resetting the TTLs. The avalanche happens not at the TTL expiration but at the **batch run time itself**: the batch job fetches all keys from the database (spiking DB load), writes them to the cache (spiking cache write load), and during the batch run, the database is overwhelmed by the batch's read queries. Additionally, if the batch job runs while the previous batch's keys are still alive (TTL not yet expired), the cache may evict the old keys to make room for the new ones, causing a brief spike in misses during the swap. The fixes: (1) **Rate-limit the batch job** — cap the batch's read rate at e.g., 1000 queries/sec, so a 100,000-key batch takes 100 seconds (not 1 second of 100k QPS). This is the most important fix. (2) **Run the batch during off-peak hours** — schedule it at 3am when traffic is low, so the database has spare capacity for the batch. (3) **Use the never-expire pattern instead of daily batch refresh** — refresh keys continuously in the background (rate-limited), not in a daily batch. This eliminates the synchronized batch load entirely. (4) **Incremental refresh** — instead of rewriting all keys daily, refresh only the keys that have changed (via a `updated_at > last_refresh` query). This reduces the batch size dramatically. (5) **Offload the batch to a read replica** — point the batch job at a read replica instead of the primary database. The lesson: TTL jitter handles synchronized *expirations*, but not synchronized *writes* — the batch job's write pattern is itself a load spike, and must be rate-limited regardless of the TTL strategy.
**Visual:**
```
Daily batch job (3am), 100k keys, TTL=3600+rand(0,600):

  T=3:00:00  Batch starts: SELECT * FROM products -> 100k rows (DB spike!)
  T=3:00:01  Batch writes 100k keys to cache (cache write spike!)
             -> DB at 100% CPU for 1 second (the batch query)
  T=3:00:01  Batch ends, cache has 100k keys with jittered TTLs
  T=4:00     First key expires (jitter=0) -> 1 DB query
  T=4:00..4:10 Remaining keys expire, spread -> ~170/sec DB load (safe)
  T=4:10     All keys expired, cache empty
  ...        (steady state, DB load low)
  T=3:00:00  Next day: batch runs again -> DB spike again (the problem)

Fix: rate-limit the batch to 1k/sec, run at 3am, offload to read replica:
  T=3:00:00  Batch starts, rate-limited 1k/sec -> DB load 1k QPS (safe)
  T=3:01:40  Batch ends (100s), cache has 100k keys
  -> No DB spike, no avalanche
```
